messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was sixty-six years old when he first described the cold to his wife, though he had been running from it for fifty-eight years. The cold itself was not the trauma—it was the herald. When his father's hands came down on him, they came with a particular temperature, a specific shock that had nothing to do with season or weather. His father had kept his hands in ice water in the garage. Marcus remembered the sound of the lid of the cooler closing, the methodical way his father would walk back inside the house, the way his mother would find an errand elsewhere. The beatings happened in the basement, where the concrete stayed cold year-round, where Marcus learned that cold on skin meant pain was coming. He was eight years old the first time, and he was still eight years old every time he felt that temperature again.

In his sixties now, Marcus worked remotely as a senior software engineer for a financial services firm. His home office was climate-controlled to seventy-two degrees precisely. He had not set foot in an office building in three years. When the air conditioning kicked in—a sudden shift, a draft across his arm or neck—his heart would begin to race before his conscious mind had even registered the temperature change. His body knew what his mind was trying to forget. The pounding in his chest would come first, a wild percussion that made him certain something terrible was about to happen, and only then would the thought arrive: *He's coming. He's getting his hands wet. He's coming down the stairs.* The memory would surface whole and unbidden, not as narrative but as sensation—the cold, the helplessness, the smell of motor oil and concrete dust.

These moments had begun to structure his life in ways he no longer questioned. He avoided looking at his own body, had done so for years. In the shower, he kept his eyes fixed on the tile wall or closed them entirely. He did not stand shirtless. The sight of his own skin seemed to trigger the same cascade of alarm that the temperature did, as if his body itself were a threat he needed to monitor and contain. His wife, Patricia, had learned not to touch him without warning. When she reached for his hand or his shoulder, she would announce it first, speak his name, give him time to brace himself. Even so, unexpected contact—a brush against him in the kitchen, her hand on his back as she passed—sent a jolt of alarm through him so acute it left him breathless. His startle response had become legendary in their marriage, a thing they managed around rather than addressed.

The social isolation had accumulated gradually. Friends from their neighborhood, couples they had known for decades, had begun to drift away. Marcus could not bear to see them. The people who had known him before—before this, before the cold, before his body had become a thing that betrayed him—they represented a kind of witness he could not tolerate. To be in their presence was to feel permanently marked, set apart, as though they could see the damage written across him. He had come to believe that people could not be trusted with this knowledge, that his only safety lay in distance. He had stopped accepting dinner invitations. He made excuses. Patricia had stopped making them.

What brought him finally to seek help was a panic attack in his own home, one so severe that Patricia had called an ambulance. The paramedics had touched him without warning—hands on his chest, on his arm—and he had fought them with a strength that shocked them both. Afterward, sitting in the emergency room, cleared of any cardiac event, Marcus had felt something shift. He was sixty-six years old. He had spent nearly six decades running from a man who had died when Marcus was thirty-two. The cold was still coming. His heart was still racing. And he was still, always, waiting for the basement door to open.
